newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Benpres issues derivatives to raise money.
newsitem.headline: Benpres issues derivatives to raise money.

text.p: Benpres Holdings Inc said on Tuesday it issued derivatives to raise $60 million, a move analysts viewed as the first indication of how difficult it was for Philippine firms to attract money after the de facto peso devaluation.
The firm announced in a statement to the Philippine Stock Exchange that it had sold derivatives based on underlying shares of Philippine Commercial International Bank (PCIBank).
Benpres Holdings has an 18 percent stake in PCIBank.

"Benpres ... informs the exchange that it has entered into a series of transactions to monetise the value of a portion of its listed shareholdings in PCIBank. Benpres raised $60 million through these transactions and intends to make available the proceeds to its operating companies," the statement said.
A company spokesman declined to elaborate on the statement saying the rest of the information was "proprietary".
Analysts said it was most likely the derivatives were sold to one of the companies within the group, probably the unlisted Lopez Inc controlled by the Lopez family.
"Who else will give you $60 million and still let you enjoy all the benefits of the shares?" said Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.
Benpres' statement said: "The transactions have been structured such that the corporation's ownership, voting rights and rights to dividends remain with the corporation."
Benpres Holdings also has investments in telephone company Bayan Telecommunications Holdings Corp and infrastructure firm First Philippine Infrastructure Development Corp.
Until recently, it held 71 percent of television firm ABS-CBN Inc but the stake was transferred to Lopez Inc.
Benpres and a French firm recently won a 25-year concession to run a part of Manila's waterworks and sewerage system, a project expected to involve major investments.
Analysts said Benpres was in need of cash for the waterworks system as well as projects undertaken by its infrastucture firm.
Reyes said it would have been difficult for Benpres to raise money in the current jittery market conditions after the peso was effectively devalued last week.
Last Thursday, another Benpres group company, First Philippine Holdings Corp, said it was postponing a proposed $300 million euroconvertible note issue.

"Due to current adverse market conditions prevailing for Philippine issues, the corporation and Deutsche Morgan Grenfell have decided to postpone the proposed convertible issue until conditions improve," First Philippine Holdings said.

The announcement came just a day before the Philippines caved in to unbearable pressure from speculators and said it would allow the peso to move in a wider range. The de facto devaluation saw the peso plunge by 11.5 percent.
On Tuesday, major Philippine banks raised their prime lending rates to 32-35 percent from 21-22 percent last week.
In such conditions, Benpres could not have sought debt as the interest costs would be prohibitive and issuing new shares was not desirable because it would dilute earnings per share, analysts said.
